title: Vivekananda's drunk monkey
hookLine: a monk in New York tells Americans their mind is a drunk monkey, then defines yoga
carry: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings
tomorrow: when the lake goes still, who is looking?

cards: New York, 1895. A young monk from Calcutta, Swami Vivekananda, has taken rooms in the city and is teaching small classes to Americans who have barely heard the word yoga. He doesn't start with poses.
He tells them about a monkey. A monkey is restless by nature. Now someone gives it wine, so it's drunk.
Then a scorpion stings it. Then a demon gets into it. That, he says, is the human mind: drunk on desire, stung by jealousy, seized by pride.
And the line he keeps coming back to is Patanjali's second.

teach.b: Here it is: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind.

teach.h: CHITTA, VRITTI, NIRODHA: MIND, TURNING, STILL.
teach.b: Chitta is the mind in the widest sense: thinking, feeling, remembering. Vritti means a turning, a whirl, from a root that means to turn, like a wheel: the thoughts, the moods, the commentary that never stops.
Nirodha means stilling, restraining, bringing to rest.

teach.h: NOT ONE WORD ABOUT THE BODY.
teach.b: Four words, and not one is about the body. That's the heart of yoga as a Hindu teaching: it's a discipline of the mind.
Posture gets only a few threads in the whole book, and most poses taught in classes today grew up much later.
Vivekananda gave his students a second picture, a lake. When wind ripples it, you can't see the bottom. When the water goes still, you see all the way down.
Why would a Hindu want to see the bottom?
Because of what's under the ripples. Patanjali calls it the seer; the Upanishads call it atman, the self.
Nirodha can be read as restraint, even cessation, but many teachers hear it as a settling, water going still, not a lid slammed down. And the drunk monkey isn't hopeless.

teach.h: YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE MIND'S TURNINGS.
teach.b: Vivekananda's advice: don't fight it. Let it jump, and watch. Day by day, he said, it gets calmer.

how: Students of the Yoga Sutras often memorize 1.2 in Sanskrit, and many yoga teachers in India and abroad quote it as the definition of yoga before teaching any posture.

o: a breath counted slowly in and out
a turning or ripple of the mind
a pose held still in yoga practice

games.q: the monkey and the definition — tap the pairs.
p: Vivekananda's picture of the restless mind
you can see to the bottom

s: Patanjali defines yoga as a set of physical poses
his definition is about the mind: the stilling of its turnings.
Vivekananda taught Patanjali's yoga to classes in New York in the 1890s
and he started with a restless monkey, not a pose.
nirodha means forcing every thought out of your head
many teachers read it as settling, like water going still, not a lid slammed down.

games.q: your mind is the drunk monkey today: texts, worries, a song. what does Vivekananda say to do with it?
o: let it jump, and watch it, until it settles.
give up: yoga is for calm people.
games.why: let the monkey jump and watch; it calms day by day. yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings, not a fight.

practice: Sit and let the monkey jump: don't chase it and don't scold it, just watch where it goes, a text, a sound, a small worry.

Picture each one as wind on a lake, crossing the surface and passing, and when the water is flat for a moment between them, rest there. If you pray, you can let that stillness be your prayer; if you don't, let it simply be quiet.

wordCard.voice: Vritti, a turning of the mind. Yoga is the stilling of these turnings: chitta, vritti, nirodha. Mind, turning, stillness.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Yoga Sutra 1.2: chitta, mind + vritti, turning (root vrit, to turn) + nirodha, stilling.

carryVoice: Your line: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Not your toes. The monkey. Day two ninety-six.

sources.ref: Swami Vivekananda, Raja Yoga (1896), from his New York classes: the mind as a monkey drunk with desire, stung by jealousy and possessed by pride; letting the mind run and watching it; the lake image
